title: Compare the rate-limiting algorithms — fixed-window counter (simple but allows a ~2× burst at the window boundary), sliding-window log/counter (smooths that boundary burst at higher memory cost), token bucket (allows controlled bursts up to the bucket size with steady refill), and leaky bucket (enforces a constant outflow rate) — and how do you enforce the limit consistently across many instances (a shared counter in Redis)?

s1_definition.profdef: The four classic rate-limiting algorithms trade simplicity, accuracy, memory, and burst behavior differently. The fixed-window counter counts requests per fixed clock window and is simplest but allows up to a double burst at window boundaries. The sliding-window log keeps timestamps for exact trailing-window counts at high memory cost, while the sliding-window counter approximates that cheaply by blending the current and previous window, smoothing the boundary burst. The token bucket refills tokens at a steady rate up to a capacity, permitting controlled bursts while enforcing a long-run average. The leaky bucket drains requests at a constant rate, smoothing bursty input into a steady output stream. Across many instances, consistency requires a shared, atomic counter, typically in Redis, so the limit is enforced globally rather than per instance.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India limits how many forms a customer can submit. The fixed-window counter is like resetting the tally at the top of every hour: a clever customer submits a batch at 10:59 and another at 11:00, sneaking in almost double right at the boundary. The sliding window is like a guard who looks back over the last sixty minutes continuously rather than at the clock hour, so there is no boundary trick; keeping a note of every single submission time is accurate but heavy, while a cheaper approximation blends this hour and last hour. The token bucket is like giving the customer a jar of ten tokens that refills slowly: they can spend a quick burst of ten at once, then must wait as the jar refills. The leaky bucket is like a funnel that drips forms through at a fixed steady rate no matter how fast they are poured in. And because the bank has many branches, all of them must consult one central tally so a customer cannot multiply the limit by visiting every branch.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fixed window is simplest but allows a boundary double-burst, sliding window smooths that at memory cost, token bucket allows controlled bursts, leaky bucket enforces constant outflow — and across instances you must share the counter in Redis atomically.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The four classic rate-limiting algorithms trade simplicity, accuracy, memory, and burst behavior differently. The fixed-window counter counts requests per fixed clock window and is simplest but allows up to a double burst at window boundaries. The sliding-window log keeps timestamps for exact trailing-window counts at high memory cost, while the sliding-window counter approximates that cheaply by blending the current and previous window, smoothing the boundary burst. The token bucket refills tokens at a steady rate up to a capacity, permitting controlled bursts while enforcing a long-run average. The leaky bucket drains requests at a constant rate, smoothing bursty input into a steady output stream. Across many instances, consistency requires a shared, atomic counter, typically in Redis, so the limit is enforced globally rather than per instance.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India limits how many forms a customer can submit. The fixed-window counter is like resetting the tally at the top of every hour: a clever customer submits a batch at 10:59 and another at 11:00, sneaking in almost double right at the boundary. The sliding window is like a guard who looks back over the last sixty minutes continuously rather than at the clock hour, so there is no boundary trick; keeping a note of every single submission time is accurate but heavy, while a cheaper approximation blends this hour and last hour. The token bucket is like giving the customer a jar of ten tokens that refills slowly: they can spend a quick burst of ten at once, then must wait as the jar refills. The leaky bucket is like a funnel that drips forms through at a fixed steady rate no matter how fast they are poured in. And because the bank has many branches, all of them must consult one central tally so a customer cannot multiply the limit by visiting every branch.

**One line to remember:** Fixed window is simplest but allows a boundary double-burst, sliding window smooths that at memory cost, token bucket allows controlled bursts, leaky bucket enforces constant outflow — and across instances you must share the counter in Redis atomically.

sections.s2_technical:
The fixed-window counter divides time into equal windows, say one minute, and keeps a per-client counter that resets at each window boundary. Each request increments the counter, and once it reaches the limit, further requests in that window are rejected. It is trivial to implement and cheap in memory, needing just a counter and a window key. Its well-known flaw is the boundary burst: because the counter resets abruptly, a client can send a full limit's worth at the very end of one window and another full limit's worth at the very start of the next, producing up to twice the intended rate in a short span straddling the boundary. For a limit of a hundred per minute, that means up to two hundred requests in a couple of seconds around the reset.

The sliding-window log fixes the boundary problem exactly by storing a timestamp for every request and, on each new request, counting how many timestamps fall within the trailing window, discarding older ones. This is perfectly accurate because the window truly slides, but it is memory-expensive, since you store one entry per request, which for high volumes becomes large. The sliding-window counter is the practical compromise: it keeps just two counters, the current window and the previous window, and estimates the rate by weighting the previous window's count by how much of it still overlaps the trailing window. This smooths the boundary burst to a small approximation error while using almost no memory, which is why it is a popular production choice.

The token bucket models a bucket that holds up to a capacity of tokens and refills at a steady rate, say ten tokens per second up to a capacity of twenty. Each request removes one token; if a token is available the request proceeds, otherwise it is rejected or queued. Because the bucket can hold accumulated tokens up to its capacity, it permits a controlled burst up to that capacity when the client has been idle, then settles to the refill rate for sustained traffic. This burst tolerance is often exactly what you want for real user traffic, which is naturally bursty, while still bounding the long-run average. The leaky bucket is the mirror image focused on output smoothing: requests enter a queue and are processed, or leak out, at a fixed constant rate regardless of how bursty the arrivals are. It enforces a strictly smooth outflow, which is ideal when a downstream system can only handle a steady rate, though it offers no burst allowance and may add queuing delay or drop overflow.

Choosing among them is about the behavior you want. Fixed window when you need dead-simple and can tolerate boundary bursts. Sliding window when you need accuracy without boundary bursts, picking the log for exactness or the counter for low memory. Token bucket when you want to allow natural bursts while capping the average, which is the most common API choice. Leaky bucket when you must protect a downstream with a strictly constant rate.

The distributed enforcement question cuts across all four. If each service instance keeps its own counter or bucket in local memory, then N instances each allow the full limit and the effective limit is N times too high. To enforce the limit for the whole system, the state must live in a shared store that every instance consults, and Redis is the standard choice because it is fast and supports atomic operations. The update must be atomic to avoid races where two instances both read a stale value and overshoot, which in practice means a Redis Lua script that performs the read, refill or count, check, and update in one indivisible server-side step. For a distributed token bucket you store the token count and last-refill timestamp per key and run a Lua script to refill-and-consume atomically; for a sliding-window counter you store the two window counts; for fixed window an INCR with EXPIRE suffices. The senior-level nuances are that Redis is now on the critical path so it must be highly available, that you should return a 429 with a Retry-After header, that clock skew across instances is handled by letting Redis be the single clock source inside the script, and that you often layer limits and provide a conservative local fallback if the shared store is briefly unreachable so a limiter outage does not take down the API.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India wants to pick the right rate-limiting algorithm for its transfer API and enforce it across many gateway instances.

Problem 1 — the team first used a fixed-window counter set to a hundred per minute, and a scripted client discovered it could fire a hundred transfers at 10:59:59 and another hundred at 11:00:01, pushing two hundred through in two seconds and briefly overloading the transfer service. This is exactly the fixed-window boundary burst, and it motivates comparing the alternatives.

Problem 2 — switching to a sliding-window log fixed the burst but stored a timestamp per request, and under heavy load the memory grew uncomfortably. This is exactly the memory cost of the log, and it motivates the sliding-window counter approximation.

Problem 3 — the bank actually wanted to allow a genuine small burst (a user making a few quick transfers) while capping the average, which pointed to a token bucket, and separately it needed a strictly steady feed into a legacy settlement system, which pointed to a leaky bucket. And because there were several gateway instances, whichever algorithm was chosen had to share its state in Redis so the limit was global.

The mini-project builds a `RateLimiter` interface with `FixedWindowLimiter`, `SlidingWindowCounterLimiter`, `TokenBucketLimiter`, and `LeakyBucketLimiter`, plus a note on backing each with a shared Redis store. The demo feeds each algorithm the same adversarial boundary-straddling request pattern and a bursty pattern, and prints how many each admits and rejects, making the differences visible side by side.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a limit of five per one-second window, an adversarial pattern of five requests at nine hundred ninety-nine milliseconds followed by five more just two milliseconds later at one thousand one milliseconds, and a burst pattern of eight requests all at the same instant with refill or leak of five per second and capacity five.

Step 1: For the fixed-window limiter, the first five requests at nine hundred ninety-nine milliseconds fall in window one and are all admitted, reaching the limit of five. Two milliseconds later the clock crosses into window two, the counter resets abruptly, and the next five requests are also admitted. So ten requests slipped through in a two-millisecond span, demonstrating the roughly double boundary burst.

Step 2: For the sliding-window counter on the same pattern, the first five at nine hundred ninety-nine milliseconds are admitted and recorded in the current window. When the window rolls just two milliseconds later, the previous count of five is carried and weighted by the overlap, which is almost the entire window, so the smoothed estimate is near five already. The next requests push the estimate past the limit and are rejected, so far fewer than ten are admitted. The boundary burst is smoothed away.

Step 3: For the token bucket on the burst of eight instant requests, the bucket starts full at capacity five. Because all eight arrive at the same instant with no time for refill, the first five each consume a token and are admitted as a controlled burst up to the capacity, and the remaining three find the bucket empty and are rejected.

Step 4: For the leaky bucket on the same burst of eight, the bucket capacity is five and no time passes for leaking, so the first five drops fit and are admitted while the sixth through eighth overflow and are rejected. The difference in spirit is that the leaky bucket is about a steady drain over time, so sustained input would be shaped to exactly five per second regardless of arrival burstiness.

Step 5: The demo then states the distributed requirement explicitly: any of these algorithms must be backed by a shared counter in Redis using an atomic Lua script, so that N gateway instances enforce one global limit rather than each allowing the full limit.

Step 6: The side-by-side output makes the comparison concrete: fixed window admitted about double at the boundary, sliding window smoothed it, token and leaky both capped the instant burst to the bucket size, and the closing note ties it to distributed enforcement.

```
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    === Boundary-burst test (limit=5/sec) ===
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    fixed-window: admitted 10 in a 2ms span (fixed allows ~2x, sliding smooths)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    sliding-window-counter: admitted 5 in a 2ms span (fixed allows ~2x, sliding smooths)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    === Burst test: 8 instant requests (refill/leak=5/sec, cap=5) ===
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    token-bucket: admitted 5/8 instant (token allows burst up to capacity, leaky caps to bucket)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    leaky-bucket: admitted 5/8 instant (token allows burst up to capacity, leaky caps to bucket)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    DISTRIBUTED: back ANY of these with a SHARED Redis counter (atomic Lua)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    so N instances enforce ONE global limit, not N x limit.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
There are four classic rate-limiting algorithms, and I compare them on simplicity, memory, accuracy, and burst behavior. The fixed-window counter is the simplest: it counts requests per fixed clock window and resets at each boundary. It needs almost no memory, but its well-known flaw is the boundary burst, because a client can send a full limit at the very end of one window and another full limit at the very start of the next, producing up to twice the intended rate in a short span straddling the reset. For a hundred per minute that is up to two hundred in a couple of seconds.

The sliding window fixes that boundary problem. The sliding-window log stores a timestamp for every request and counts those in the trailing window, which is perfectly accurate but memory-heavy because you keep one entry per request. The sliding-window counter is the practical compromise: it keeps just the current and previous window counts and weights the previous one by how much of it still overlaps the trailing window, which smooths the boundary burst to a small approximation error while using almost no memory, so it is a popular production choice. The token bucket takes a different angle: it refills tokens at a steady rate up to a capacity, and each request consumes a token, so it permits a controlled burst up to the bucket size when a client has been idle and then settles to the refill rate. That burst tolerance matches how real user traffic actually behaves, which is why it is the most common choice for public APIs. The leaky bucket is the mirror image focused on output: requests drain at a constant fixed rate regardless of how bursty the arrivals are, so it enforces a strictly smooth outflow, which is ideal when a downstream system can only handle a steady feed, at the cost of no burst allowance and possible queuing delay.

So the selection rule I give is: fixed window when you need dead-simple and can tolerate a boundary burst, sliding window when you need accuracy without that burst, choosing the log for exactness or the counter for low memory, token bucket when you want to allow natural bursts while capping the average, and leaky bucket when you must protect a downstream with a strictly constant rate. We actually walked this path on our transfer API: a fixed window let a scripted client double-burst at the minute boundary, a sliding-window log fixed it but grew memory under load, so we settled on a token bucket for the user-facing limit because it allowed a genuine small burst while capping the average, and a leaky bucket where we fed a legacy settlement system that needed a steady rate.

The distributed enforcement point cuts across all four and is where most candidates slip. If each instance keeps its own counter in local memory, then N instances each allow the full limit and the effective limit is N times too high. To enforce one global limit, the state must live in a shared store that every instance consults, and Redis is the standard because it is fast and supports atomic operations. The update must be atomic, which in practice means a Redis Lua script that reads, refills or rolls or leaks, checks, and updates in one indivisible server-side step, so two instances can never both read a stale value and overshoot. A nice side benefit is that Redis becomes the single clock source inside the script, which sidesteps clock skew across instances.

The way I close it for an interviewer is that fixed window is simplest but bursts at the boundary, sliding window smooths that at some memory cost, token bucket allows controlled bursts, and leaky bucket forces a constant outflow, and whichever I choose, I back it with a shared atomic counter in Redis so the limit holds globally across every instance, I return a 429 with Retry-After, keep Redis highly available since it is on the critical path, and provide a conservative local fallback so a limiter outage never takes down the API.
